chapterTitle: Brain Stem, Cranial Cavity, Temporal Region, and Pterygopalatine Fossa

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is Not characterizing the pyramidal tract?
options: It terminates on AHCs and cranial nerve nuclei
90% of it cross to opposite side at medulla
It is only one neuron from cortex to AHCs
questions.explanation: The pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth (infants have primitive reflexes but lack voluntary control); it matures over the first two years as corticospinal fibers fully develop.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal tract is not fully functional at birth.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The only cranial nerve that decussates before its emergence is:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates (crosses) in the brainstem before emerging from the dorsal surface of the midbrain. This is unique among cranial nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that decussates before emergence

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: During the cotton wool test for crude touch, the receptors responsible are:
questions.explanation: Mechanoreceptors detect the light touch sensation tested by cotton wool; they include Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal arcuate fibers are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (crossing fibers from gracile and cuneate nuclei) are present in the CLOSED MEDULLA where they sweep around the central gray to form the medial lemniscus. In the open medulla, these fibers have already crossed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in closed medulla, sweep around central gray to form medial lemniscus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tecto-spinal tract arise from:
options: superior colliculus of tectum in mid brain
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus of the midbrain tectum and descends to control reflexive head and neck movements in response to visual stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducens nucleus (CN VI) and internal genu of facial nerve - located on the floor of the 4th ventricle in the pons.选项E正确. The answer is E. It's a bulge caused by these nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: overlies abducens nucleus and facial nerve genu - floor of fourth ventricle in pons.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Somatic efferent column of nuclei includes:
questions.explanation: The nucleus that receives taste fibers is the nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus), particularly its rostral/gustatory part. It receives SVA fibers from CN VII (via chorda tympani), IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius receives taste sensation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which part of the anterior wall of the third ventricle is formed by a thin membrane derived from the telencephalon?
questions.explanation: The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle; it is a thin membrane derived from the telencephalon containing the organum vasculosum.
questions.keyConcept: Third ventricle anterior wall

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with a complaint of persistent numbness and tingling on the posterior aspect of their scalp, especially on the left side behind the ear. They report no other neurological symptoms. Which nerve is likely responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve is a branch of the cervical plexus (C2) that supplies the skin of the scalp posterior to the ear and the upper part of the lateral surface of the auricle. The greater occipital nerve (C2) supplies the posterior scalp near the midline. The posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII) supplies behind the ear.
questions.keyConcept: Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp posterior and lateral to the ear (posterolateral scalp).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Facial colliculus overlies:
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers that loop around it (the facial nerve genu). This creates a prominence in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus overlies abducent nucleus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle (midbrain) would present with:
options: Loss of fine touch on the left side of the body
Loss of pain sensation on the right side
Skeletal motor loss on the entire left side
questions.explanation: Right cerebral peduncle lesion causes left-sided motor weakness (contralateral) because corticospinal fibers have already crossed at the pyramidal decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle lesion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) forms the anterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. It contains the corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri forms anterolateral boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei, located in the midbrain, contains general visceral efferent (GVE) fibers?
questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (accessory oculomotor nucleus) is located in the midbrain and contains preganglionic parasympathetic neurons that supply the ciliary and sphincter pupillae muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to intraocular muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The final neurons in the auditory pathway are cells of:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body contains the final neurons of the auditory pathway, projecting via the acoustic radiation to the primary auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway final neurons

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Second order neuron starts in ....... goes via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons in the crude touch pathway start in the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus) of the spinal cord and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch second neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is related to the anterior corticospinal tract?
options: Supplies the muscles of the trunk
questions.explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract arises from the medial precentral cortex, descends without decussating in the spinal cord, and terminates on interneurons controlling proximal muscles and axial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior corticospinal tract is uncrossed, controlling axial and proximal limb muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT:
options: In the lower part, there are motor decussation.
At a higher level, there are sensory decussation.
Contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.explanation: In the closed medulla, the main inferior olivary nucleus is present, and it contains the gracile and cuneate nuclei on the dorsal aspect. The motor decussation is in the lower part, and sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers) is at a higher level - making 'higher level has sensory decussation' TRUE, not the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: motor decussation lower, sensory decussation at higher level

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cavity of the mesencephalon is:
questions.explanation: The cavity of the mesencephalon is the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalon cavity: cerebral aqueduct.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning the fourth ventricle; choose the most correct answer:
options: Its floor is formed by the closed medulla and pons.
Its roof is formed by the superior and inferior medullary vela.
Its choroids plexus is present in the floor of the ventricle.
It has a communication with the lateral ventricle.
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle roof is formed by the superior cerebellar peduncle (superior medullary velum) and inferior medullary velum, not the floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In dorsal surface of medulla oblongata, choose CORRECT statement:
options: Gracile tubercle is the most medial structure of open medulla.
Base of open medulla is formed by medullary stria.
Vestibular trigone lies between limbs of inferior fovea.
Hypoglossal trigone forms most medial trigone of superior fovea.
Apex of open medulla is continuous with cerebral aqueduct.
questions.explanation: The vestibular trigone lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This is the correct statement about dorsal medullary surface features.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular trigone between limbs of inferior fovea

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior spinal artery supplies the following structures Except:
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord including the anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Gracile and cuneate nuclei are supplied by medullary branches of:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei (dorsal column nuclei) are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, not the anterior spinal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal/PICA supply dorsal column nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The aqueduct of Sylvius connects which of the following ventricular structures?
questions.explanation: The aqueduct of Sylvius connects the third ventricle (above) to the fourth ventricle (below) in the midbrain. It passes through the cerebral peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects third and fourth ventricles, passing through the midbrain.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nucleus is:
options: A group of cell bodies within peripheral nervous system.
A group of cell bodies within central nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within peripheral nervous system.
A group of nerve fibers within central nervous system.
A collection of nerve fibers in brain stem.
questions.explanation: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the CNS. A ganglion is the equivalent in the PNS. Nerve fibers form tracts or nerves, not nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus = cluster of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards cranial nerve attachment to brain stem, choose the CORRECT matching:
options: Hypoglossal nerve - posterolateral sulcus of medulla.
Vagus nerve - groove between pyramid & olive.
Facial nerve - lower border of pons above pyramid.
questions.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve attaches at the cerebellopontine angle, which is the angle between the pons, cerebellum, and medulla. This is the correct matching for the anatomical location.
questions.keyConcept: CN VIII at cerebellopontine angle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is present in the ventral surface of the medulla?
questions.explanation: The ventral medullary surface contains the pyramids (corticospinal tracts) and the olives (inferior olivary nucleus). The dorsal surface shows the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus.
questions.keyConcept: Medullary pyramids contain decussating corticospinal fibers; olives contain inferior olivary nuclei.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The reticular activating system (RAS) is best described by which statement?
options: Its neurons are located only in the medulla oblongata.
Its neurons can be activated by sensory signals from proprioceptors.
Its activity is decreased by stress.
It discharges inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons.
questions.explanation: The RAS receives sensory input from proprioceptors and various sensory modalities to maintain cortical arousal and alertness.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular activating system

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal (back) aspect of the brainstem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as it exits dorsally from the midbrain (just below the inferior colliculus) after decussating in the superior medullary velum. All other cranial nerves exit ventrally.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve with dorsal exit from the midbrain after decussation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (GVE - General Visceral Efferent) that innervate cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal organs.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus: GVE (parasympathetic preganglionic)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Head rotation in response to visual stimuli, with crossing at the level of the superior colliculus, is mediated by which tract?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract decussates at the superior medullary velum (rostral medulla), which is at the level of the midbrain-pons junction, not the midbrain itself.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract decussates at the level of the inferior colliculus/superior medullary velum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nucleus ventralis posterior of thalamus receives the following Except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus ventralis posterior (VP) of the thalamus receives medial lemniscus (body tactile/proprioceptive), spinal lemniscus (body pain/temperature), trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation), and fibers from nucleus solitarius (gustatory). The lateral lemniscus carries auditory information to the inferior colliculus, NOT to VP nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: VP nucleus receives medial lemniscus, spinal lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus, and gustatory fibers; lateral lemniscus goes to inferior colliculus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is present at the level of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract (carrying pallidal and cerebellar projections) is present at midbrain level, running between red nucleus and inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Midbrain structures

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures connects the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Magendie is the median aperture connecting the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space (cisterna magna), allowing CSF flow from the ventricle to the basal cisterns.
questions.keyConcept: Median aperture (Magendie) connects fourth ventricle to subarachnoid space at the cisterna magna.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the attachment of the cranial nerves to the brain stem, choose the INCORRECT matching:
options: Hypoglossal nerve - sulcus between olive & ICP.
Trigeminal nerve - Junction of MCP & basis pontis.
Oculomotor nerve - medial side of crus cerebri.
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve attaches in the sulcus between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle. This is a posterior attachment, not between pyramid and olive. The statement is incorrect about the groove location.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII between olive and ICP

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve sends afferent fibers to the nucleus solitarius?
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal), and X (vagus) send afferent (taste and visceral) fibers to the nucleus solitarius. The vagus nerve carries the largest contribution of visceral information.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus receives visceral and taste afferents from CN VII, IX, and X.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic onion-like lamellar structure located in dermis and deeper tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following is not true concerning tricyclic antidepressant toxicity:
options: Convulsions is one of the features of toxicity.
Conduction defects are responsible for the arrhythmia.
questions.explanation: Atropine toxicity IS seen in TCA toxicity - this is NOT true. Option C is incorrect. TCA toxicity causes prominent anticholinergic effects (mydriasis, dry skin, urinary retention, hyperthermia). Arrhythmias (A) occur and are managed with NaHCO3. Convulsions (B) are common. Conduction defects (D) cause arrhythmias.
questions.keyConcept: TCA toxicity presents with anticholinergic signs, cardiac arrhythmias, and seizures requiring specific management.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Trigeminal lemniscus is present in:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) is present in the medulla and pons, carrying facial sensory information to the VPM thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal lemniscus location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following cranial nerves is attached to the back of the brain stem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve to attach to the posterior (dorsal) surface of the brain stem. It emerges from the posterior aspect of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve is only CN from posterior brainstem

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is responsible for fine skilled movements of the index finger?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract originates from motor cortex including the precentral gyrus and premotor areas. The hand representation in area 4 controls skilled finger movements through lateral corticospinal fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Skilled hand movements are mediated by corticospinal neurons in the precentral gyrus hand area.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cauda equina is composed of:
options: The lower part of the spinal cord
Dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerves
questions.explanation: The cauda equina (horse's tail) consists of the dorsal and ventral roots of the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves traveling within the subarachnoid space below L1-2.
questions.keyConcept: Cauda equina: dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral, coccygeal nerves.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In a neurological examination, while performing cotton wool test:
options: The sensation tested is fine touch.
The sensation tested is carried on C fibers only.
The receptors are moderately adapting receptors.
The cotton is felt better on the palmar side of the hands.
questions.explanation: The cotton wool test assesses fine touch (discriminative touch) using Meissner's corpuscles and hair follicle receptors that are moderate adaptors, particularly sensitive on glabrous skin like fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Cotton wool test: fine/discriminative touch via mechanoreceptors (Meissner's corpuscles).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Neural crest gives all the following Except:
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is a motor relay center in the midbrain that develops from the NEUROEPITHELIUM of the midbrain, NOT from neural crest. Neural crest derivatives include spinal ganglia (sensory), arachnoid mater, suprarenal medulla (chromaffin cells), and sympathetic ganglia. This makes B the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Red nucleus from midbrain neuroepithelium, NOT neural crest. Neural crest gives: spinal ganglia, arachnoid, adrenal medulla, sympathetic ganglia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the limbic system?
options: It is involved in emotion and memory.
questions.explanation: The limbic system, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus, is fundamentally involved in emotional processing and memory formation, particularly through connections with the hypothalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic system: emotion and memory processing.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: At birth, the conus medullaris ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: At birth, the conus medullaris is located at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). It ascends to L1–L2 by adulthood due to differential growth.
questions.keyConcept: Birth conus medullaris at L3; ascends to L1–L2 in adults

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has a tumor in the fourth ventricle. Which cranial nerve nucleus is most likely affected due to its location?
questions.explanation: The abducens nucleus (CN VI) is located in the floor of the fourth ventricle, near the facial colliculus. A fourth ventricle tumor would most likely affect the abducens nerve, which has a long intracranial course.
questions.keyConcept: Abducens nucleus in the pons is vulnerable to fourth ventricle masses due to its dorsal location.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The fourth ventricle is connected to the third ventricle by:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is the narrow channel that passes through the midbrain and connects the third ventricle anteriorly with the fourth ventricle posteriorly. It is flanked by the cerebral peduncles and is the most common site of obstruction in non-communicating hydrocephalus.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct connects 3rd ventricle (anterior) with 4th ventricle (posterior).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 44-year-old female patient has a lesion in the right cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. She would present with a loss of:
options: fine touch and pain sensation from the entire left side of the body
fine touch and pain sensation from the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire right side of the body
skeletal motor control to both sides of the body
skeletal motor control to the entire left side of the body
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract decussates at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. After decussation, the fibers descend in the lateral column of the spinal cord. A right cerebral peduncle lesion affects fibers that have NOT yet decussated, therefore causing CONTRALATERAL (left-sided) motor weakness. The corticospinal fibers to the lower limb are most medial in the peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle contains corticospinal fibers BEFORE their decussation in the medulla; right peduncle lesion = LEFT-sided weakness.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nucleus contains both general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA) fibers?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla contains both GVA (visceral sensation including baroreceptor and chemoreceptor input) and SVA (taste) fibers, making it unique in having both modalities.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus processes both visceral afferent and special visceral afferent (taste) information.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei represents the somatic efferent column?
questions.explanation: This matching tests nuclei: facial nucleus - facial muscles; nucleus ambiguus - pharyngeal muscles; dorsal motor nucleus of X - visceral organs. All are branchiomotor or visceral motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Choose the correct order of CSF circulation:
options: Third ventricle, lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Lateral ventricles, fourth ventricle, third ventricle, central canal.
Lateral ventricles, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, subarachnoid space.
Fourth ventricle, third ventricle, lateral ventricles, central canal.
questions.explanation: CSF flows from lateral ventricles through interventricular foramina to third ventricle, then through cerebral aqueduct to fourth ventricle, and finally into subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: CSF flow: lateral -> third -> fourth -> subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures lies between limbs of inferior fovea?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is a bump in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve wrapping around it. It lies between the limbs of the inferior fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus between limbs of inferior fovea

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: After falling down from a staircase, a young woman is found to have loss of voluntary movement on the right side of the body and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side below the mid thoracic region. The probable site of lesion is:
options: Transection of the right half of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of the left side of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of sensory and motor pathways on the right side of the pons
Transection of the left half of the spinal cord in the lumbar region
questions.explanation: Transection of the right half of spinal cord in upper thoracic region. Option A is correct. Right hemiplegia (right voluntary movement loss) and left pain/temperature loss indicate right Brown-Sequard syndrome. The motor fibers decussate at the cervicomedullary junction, so hemisection causes ipsilateral motor loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral motor paralysis with contralateral pain/temperature loss indicates hemisection on the side of motor deficits.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Second order Neuron start in ........., going via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons start in the medulla (gracile and cuneate nuclei) and cross to form the medial lemniscus, ascending to the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception second neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Decussation at the level of the superior midbrain occurs in which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique in that it exits the midbrain dorsally and decussates completely before emerging. The oculomotor nerve exits ventrally. Other cranial nerves exit at pontine or medullary levels.
questions.keyConcept: CN IV is the only cranial nerve that decussates and exits dorsally from the midbrain.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which sentence is NOT correct for long-term potentiation:
options: A rapid repeated brief stimulation leads to a persistent enhancement of response.
Glutamate transmitter and its NMDA receptors may play a role.
Increase Ca++ in pre and post-synaptic neurons may play a role.
Protein synthesis, growth and increased neuronal connections are possible mechanisms.
questions.explanation: LTP (long-term potentiation) is primarily involved in hippocampal learning, not cerebellar learning. The cerebellum uses a different mechanism involving LTD (long-term depression) for motor learning. LTP does involve glutamate/NMDA receptors, Ca++ increases, protein synthesis, and new connections.
questions.keyConcept: LTP: hippocampal learning (memory); LTD: cerebellar learning (motor). Both involve glutamate receptors.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sleep, all are true EXCEPT:
options: It helps brain rest and brain plasticity.
It may be due to synaptic fatigue of RAS neurons.
It may be due to active inhibition of RAS by sleep centers.
It may be due to increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus brain stem nuclei.
It may be due to accumulation of sleep inducing lipids or peptide in the CSF.
questions.explanation: Increased activity of raphe magnus and locus coeruleus PROMOTES wakefulness and arousal, not sleep. These nuclei are part of the ascending activating system.
questions.keyConcept: Raphe magnus and locus coeruleus = wakefulness/REM-on neurons; NOT sleep centers.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following is an afferent connection to the inferior colliculus:
questions.explanation: This matching tests midbrain structures: cerebral aqueduct (around which the tectal plate curves); trochlear nucleus (inferior to oculomotor); superior cerebellar peduncle (lateral to red nucleus).
questions.keyConcept: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in midbrain

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle leads to:
questions.explanation: The superior angle of the fourth ventricle is continuous with the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), which connects the third and fourth ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Superior 4th ventricle angle leads to cerebral aqueduct

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Medial eminence in floor of fourth ventricle overlies the nucleus of:
questions.explanation: The medial eminence overlies the abducent nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. The facial colliculus (a elevation) is formed by the abducent nucleus and the facial nerve fibers looping around it.
questions.keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies abducent nucleus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nucleus that receives taste fibers is:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and vertebral artery branches, not the anterior spinal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries supply dorsal column nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Acute-stage upper motor neuron lesions result in:
questions.explanation: In the ACUTE stage of upper motor neuron lesion, there is FLACCID paralysis (not spastic) due to spinal shock—loss of all reflexes and tone below the lesion. This phase lasts days to weeks. Later, as spinal shock resolves, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski sign develop. The answer choice D (flaccid paralysis) describes the acute UMN lesion phase.
questions.keyConcept: Acute UMN lesion = FLACCID paralysis (spinal shock); chronic UMN lesion = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the fourth ventricle
options: Is the cavity of hind brain
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle is the cavity of the hindbrain (rhombencephalon), communicates with third ventricle above and subarachnoid space below via median/lateral apertures, and has a roof and floor.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle features

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Decussation of internal arcuate fibres takes place in:
questions.explanation: Decussation of internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) occurs in the upper part of the closed medulla, at the level of the olivary nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory decussation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: CSF produced in the fourth ventricle flows into which subarachnoid space via its three foramina?
options: Subarachnoid space over the cerebral hemispheres
questions.explanation: CSF exits the fourth ventricle through the foramina of Luschka (lateral) and Magendie (median) into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brainstem and cerebellum (cisterna magna).
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle CSF flows through Luschka and Magendie apertures into the subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is present in the dorsal surface of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The corpora quadrigemina (superior and inferior colliculi) are on the dorsal midbrain surface. The basis pedunculi (cerebral peduncles) are on the ventral surface.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain features include the four colliculi (corpora quadrigemina) for visual and auditory reflexes.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following is not true concerning codeine:
options: Diarrhea is a troublesome side effect.
questions.explanation: Codeine side effects include constipation (not diarrhea), as it is an opioid constipating effect. It is less potent as an antitussive than morphine.
questions.keyConcept: Codeine side effects: antitussive, analgesic, constipating (not diarrheal)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nucleus is located most medially in the medulla?
questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is located most medially in the medulla, receiving visceral sensory input from vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves for taste and visceral reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Solitary nucleus is the most medial medullary nucleus, involved in visceral sensory processing.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following sentences about sleep and arousal is true:
options: Posterior hypothalamus is a Non-REM sleep center.
Cholinergic neurons of upper brain stem induce arousal.
Serotonergic brain stem neurons induce REM sleep.
Suprachasmatic nucleus is a REM sleep center.
Orexin hormone of the hypothalamus regulates brain stem nuclei activity and switches the activity between seep and arousal.
questions.explanation: Orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake switching by modulating brainstem nuclei activity. Posterior hypothalamus promotes wakefulness; cholinergic neurons induce arousal; serotonergic and noradrenergic neurons promote REM sleep at different sites.
questions.keyConcept: Orexin regulates sleep-wake balance; posterior hypothalamus = wakefulness; cholinergic = arousal; serotonergic/noradrenergic = REM.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The reticular formation is responsible for:
questions.explanation: The reticular formation in the brainstem regulates arousal, sleep-wake cycles, and consciousness through ascending reticular activating system projections to the thalamus and cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Reticular formation maintains consciousness and sleep-arousal cycles via diffuse subcortical projections.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The advantage of adding Bromocriptine to L-dopa is:
options: Activates D1 receptors improving the condition
Reduces the risk of psychosis of L-dopa
Longer t½ & rapid absorption reducing fluctuations in L-dopa response
questions.explanation: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used as an adjunct to L-dopa in Parkinson's disease. Adding it to L-dopa therapy: 1) Activates D2 receptors directly, providing additional dopaminergic effect; 2) Reduces 'on-off' fluctuations by providing more continuous dopaminergic stimulation; 3) May allow lower L-dopa doses. Option B is correct - Bromocriptine reduces the risk of psychosis because it preferentially activates D2 receptors without the D1-mediated effects that may contribute to psychotic side effects. Option A is wrong because bromocriptine activates D2, not D1 receptors. Options C and D are incorrect as bromocriptine is an adjunct, not more effective than L-dopa alone.
questions.keyConcept: Bromocriptine adjunct therapy reduces L-dopa-induced psychosis by activating D2 receptors without D1-mediated side effects.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cranial part of the accessory nerve arises from
questions.explanation: The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) arises from the nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, carrying fibers that eventually join the vagus nerve to innervate laryngeal muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory nerve nucleus ambiguus origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In long-term depression:
options: A rapid repeated brief stimulation leads to a persistent enhancement of response.
A slow, prolonged, low frequency stimulation leads to decrease strength of synaptic transmission.
A rapid tetanizing presynaptic stimulation leads to continuation of postsynaptic response after removal of the stimulus.
A noxious stimulus leads to presynaptic facilitation of a habituated pathway.
A continuous benign stimulus leads to gradual increase in response.
questions.explanation: LTD (long-term depression) involves slow, prolonged low-frequency stimulation that decreases synaptic strength. LTP involves rapid repeated tetanic stimulation that increases strength. Sensitization involves noxious stimuli causing facilitation. Classic conditioning involves CS-US pairing.
questions.keyConcept: LTD: low-frequency stimulation → decreased transmission (cerebellum). LTP: high-frequency → increased transmission (hippocampus).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the main function of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus maintains internal homeostasis through autonomic control, regulates endocrine function via pituitary connection, controls food intake, temperature, thirst, and circadian rhythms.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamus integrative functions

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning the choroid plexus; choose one best answer:
options: Is formed by a plexus of capillaries and a thin layer of cuboidal epithelium.
Is responsible for absorption of the cerebrospinal fluid.
All of the choroids plexuses are present in the floor of the ventricles.
questions.explanation: Choroid plexus is formed by a capillary network (from pia) covered by a thin layer of cuboidal epithelial cells (modified ependyma).
questions.keyConcept: Choroid plexus structure

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following concerning antiparkinsonian drugs is/are CORRECT?
options: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in emergency.
L-dopa- induced dyskinesia is reduced by carbidopa.
Benztropine reduces fluctuations in response to L-dopa.
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in Parkinson's disease emergencies (e.g., akinetic crisis), and amantadine can cause insomnia. Carbidopa does not reduce L-dopa-induced dyskinesia (dopamine agonists do). Benztropine is an anticholinergic for tremor, not fluctuations. Answer E (A and D) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine SC in emergency; amantadine-induced insomnia in Parkinson's treatment

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: How does the hypothalamus control endocrine functions Through nervous control?
options: Control of posterior pituitary gland leads to secret oxytocin & vasopressin
Control of Adrenal medulla leads to secret catecholamines
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic neurons directly control the posterior pituitary via axonal projections, releasing oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH) into systemic circulation in response to neural stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamic-posterior pituitary connection

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The internal arcuate fibers in the medulla are axons of:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are axons of second-order neurons in the dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate nuclei). They decussate in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers from gracile/cuneate nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding accessory nerve: the following statements are true Except:
options: It is a purely motor nerve.
Its cranial part takes origin from the nucleus ambiguus.
It emerges at the groove between pyramid and olive.
Its spinal part runs between investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia.
Its cranial part joins the vagus.
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve is a motor nerve. Its cranial part takes origin near the nucleus ambiguus but is distinct from it. Its spinal part runs between the investing and prevertebral layers of cervical fascia in the posterior triangle. The cranial part joins the vagus. However, the accessory nerve (both roots) does NOT emerge at the groove between the pyramid and the olive—that is the exit site of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The accessory nerve emerges lateral to the olive in the postolivary sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory nerve emerges lateral to olive (postolivary sulcus), NOT between pyramid and olive.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior spinal artery supplies all the following EXCEPT:
options: The part of medulla medial to hypoglossal nerve.
The nucleus that supplies muscles of tongue.
The fibers that carry fine touch of opposite side of body.
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior horn, lateral horn, and anterior/lateral white columns. It does NOT supply the posterior columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal does not supply posterior columns

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: First order Neuron in proprioception path way end in:
options: upper half of spinal cord then ascend as tract
questions.explanation: First order neurons in the proprioception pathway cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglion; their fibers enter the upper half of the spinal cord and ascend.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in its:
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is located in the inferior roof (posterior medullary velum), not the floor or superior roof.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following is true about gracile tract:
options: Presents only in cervical & thoracic levels of spinal cord.
Carries proprioception from the upper half of the body.
Terminates at gracile nucleus in medulla.
Arises from spinal ganglia in upper half of body.
questions.explanation: The gracile tract carries proprioception from the lower half of the body (sacral, lumbar, lower thoracic) and terminates in the gracile nucleus of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A tumor in the floor of the fourth ventricle (facial colliculus region) most directly damages which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus in the floor of the 4th ventricle overlies the abducent (CN VI) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus: facial nerve wraps around abducens nucleus in floor of fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Border cells can be found in:
questions.explanation: Border cells (meningothelial cells) are found in the arachnoid mater, forming a continuous layer adjacent to the dura.
questions.keyConcept: Border cell location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the extrapyramidal tracts?
options: They originate exclusively from the motor cortex.
They are concerned with fine skilled movements.
They influence posture and muscle tone.
They decussate only in the medulla.
questions.explanation: Extrapyramidal tracts (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal) influence muscle tone, posture, and automatic movements rather than fine skilled movements controlled by the pyramidal system.
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: regulate posture and muscle tone.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which statement regarding muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ is correct?
options: Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tension
Golgi tendon organ initiates the stretch reflex
Muscle spindle is responsible for muscle tone
Golgi tendon organ has damping function
Muscle spindle is located in the tendon
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles detect length changes and initiate stretch reflexes; Golgi tendon organs detect tension changes and provide protective inhibition. Both contribute to proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles respond to length; Golgi tendon organs respond to tension for reflexive motor control.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which nucleus is located in the special visceral efferent (SVE) column?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is located in the SVE (special visceral efferent) column and innervates muscles derived from pharyngeal arches: stylopharyngeus (IX), pharyngeal muscles (X), sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus is the SVE column nucleus for pharyngeal arch-derived muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The tract in MLB responsible for head righting reflex is:
questions.explanation: The interstitiospinal tract (from interstitial nucleus of Cajal) is primarily responsible for the head righting reflex, which maintains head position in space. The tectospinal tract is for neck reflexes in response to visual stimuli. Vestibulospinal maintains posture. Reticulospinal for autonomic functions.
questions.keyConcept: Interstitiospinal tract: from interstitial nucleus of Cajal, head righting reflex, descends in MLF.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT
options: in the lower part there are motor decussation
at a higher level there are sensory decussation
contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.explanation: The main inferior olivary nucleus is present in the OPEN (not closed) medulla, located ventrolaterally. The closed medulla contains: motor decussation (lower), sensory decussation (higher), gracile and cuneate nuclei and tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: decussations, gracile/cuneate nuclei. Open medulla: inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The primary motor cortex (area 4) is chiefly responsible for:
options: Sensory perception of limb position in space
Converting the plan into actual movement
questions.explanation: Area 4 executes movement; planning is premotor/SMA.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4): execution of voluntary movement.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the internal structure of the midbrain, choose the CORRECT matching:
options: Parieto-pontine fibers - medial 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Ventral tegmental Decussation - tegmentum at level of inferior colliculus.
Cortico-spinal tract - lateral 1/5 of crus cerebri.
Cortico-nuclear tract - middle 3/5 of crus cerebri.
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It supplies stylopharyngeus (IX), pharynx/larynx muscles (X), and sternocleidomastoid/trapezius (XI).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus - common motor for IX, X, XI

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Deep pain is typically characterized by:
options: Rapidly conducted by Aδ fibers only
questions.explanation: Deep pain (visceral or deep somatic) is poorly localized, often aching or cramping, and may be referred to distant dermatomes. It is transmitted by C fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pain is dull, poorly localized, and may be referred due to convergence of deep and superficial afferents.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which parts of the hypothalamus control autonomic responses?
options: Regulation of food intake and appetite
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus controls autonomic responses primarily through the posterior and lateral hypothalamus (sympathetic) and anterior/ventromedial regions (parasympathetic), via descending pathways to brainstem autonomic centers.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamic autonomic regulation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The main sensory nucleus of spinal cord is:
questions.explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
questions.keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Ascending sensory bundle in brain stem, end in diencephalon:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus is an ascending sensory bundle in the brainstem carrying fine touch and proprioception information, terminating in the VPL nucleus of thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture, the:
questions.explanation: The median aperture (foramen of Magendie) drains CSF into the cisterna magna.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle communicates with subarachnoid space via lateral apertures of Luschka and median aperture of Magendie.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by:
questions.explanation: The posterolateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa is formed by the cerebral peduncles. These are two large bundles of descending fibers on either side of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncles form posterolateral boundary

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of lateral spino-thalamic tract except:
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract arises from the opposite side (after crossing in the spinal cord) and ascends through all brainstem levels to the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral spinothalamic tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The second-order neuron transmitting pain and temperature sensation from the face is located in which nucleus?
questions.explanation: For pain from the face, the second-order neuron is in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (not the principal sensory nucleus). Fibers then cross and ascend as the trigeminothalamic tract to the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal trigeminal nucleus is the second-order neuron for facial pain and temperature sensation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The adult derivatives of the telencephalon are:
questions.explanation: The telencephalon develops into the cerebral hemispheres including the basal ganglia, hippocampus, and lateral ventricles, while thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain derive from diencephalon and mesencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nuclei are located in the pons?
questions.explanation: Pontine cranial nerve nuclei include: abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII), and the principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal (V). The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei are in the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: CN V, VI, VII, VIII nuclei are located in the pons; III and IV are midbrain, IX, X, XI, XII are medullary.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterior external arcuate fibers are axons of:
questions.explanation: Posterior external arcuate fibers originate from the accessory cuneate nucleus (lateral cuneate nucleus), which receives proprioceptive input from the upper limb. These fibers enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Accessory cuneate nucleus gives posterior arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following statements is true:
options: 20% of the pyramidal fibers cross in pyramidal decussation.
The first order neuron for proprioception from head is in spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve.
The ventral vestibulospinal tract passes in medial longitudinal bundle.
questions.explanation: The ventral vestibulospinal tract passes in the medial longitudinal bundle, coordinating head position and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibulospinal tract location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal arcuate fibres are present in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers (second order proprioceptive neurons crossing) are present in the closed medulla where the gracile and cuneate nuclei are located.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Concerning learning:
options: Habituation is due to increase intracellular calcium leading to augmented response.
Operant conditioning occurs by inducing a response to a neutral stimulus.
Classical conditioning occurs by stimulation of reward and punishment centers.
-ve operant conditioning means adding of something to induce learning of a specific task or behavior
questions.explanation: Sensitization occurs by presynaptic facilitation of sensory neurons. Habituation involves decreased synaptic transmission (not increased calcium) due to less neurotransmitter release. Operant conditioning uses reinforcement, not neutral stimuli. Classical conditioning pairs unconditioned and conditioned stimuli. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant.
questions.keyConcept: Habituation: decreased response to repeated benign stimulus. Sensitization: enhanced response via presynaptic facilitation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the role of the enterorhinal cortex in smell?
questions.explanation: The enterorhinal cortex (area 28) is the major gateway for neocortical information to hippocampus, critical for forming and retrieving olfactory memories and spatial memory.
questions.keyConcept: Enterorhinal cortex memory function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which area of hypothalamus is responsible for sexual behavior?
questions.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus contains structures essential for sexual behavior and mating, including the preoptic area which shows sex differences in neuron number.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: sexual behavior.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The circle of Willis lies within the ……… subarachnoid cistern.
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis lies within the interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern, surrounding the interpeduncular fossa between the cerebral peduncles.
questions.keyConcept: Circle of Willis: lies in interpeduncular subarachnoid cistern.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Luschka connects which two structures?
questions.explanation: The foramina of Luschka (lateral apertures) connect the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space at the cerebellopontine angle, allowing CSF to exit the ventricular system.
questions.keyConcept: Luschka apertures are lateral openings of fourth ventricle to subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve is not found in the open medulla?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) emerges from the pre-olivary sulcus of the closed medulla, not the open medulla. Cranial nerves IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla at the post-olivary area.
questions.keyConcept: CN XII emerges from the closed medulla; CN IX, X, XI emerge from the open medulla.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is a narrow channel passing through the midbrain that connects the third ventricle (anteriorly, at the level of the midbrain) with the fourth ventricle (posteriorly, at the pontomedullary junction). It is surrounded by the periaqueductal gray matter.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects the third and fourth ventricles, surrounded by periaqueductal gray matter.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which part of the fourth ventricle contains the choroid plexus?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus in the fourth ventricle is located in the roof (posterior/inferior border), specifically along the tela choroidea and in the lateral recesses near the foramina of Luschka.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle choroid plexus is found in the tela choroidea of the ventricular roof.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following arteries supplies the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and its branches, including the posterior communicating artery. The basilar artery supplies the upper midbrain through its superior cerebellar artery branch.
questions.keyConcept: PCA and basilar artery branches supply the midbrain via posterior circulation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of medial lemniscus except:
options: cross from opposite side to thalamus
arise from pons in brain stem
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus arises from the upper closed medulla (after crossing as internal arcuate fibers), not from the pons; it carries sensory information to the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is part of the diencephalon?
questions.explanation: The diencephalon consists of four major structures: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (including pineal gland), and subthalamus, surrounding the third ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Diencephalon: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Third order Neuron start in ......... going via ...........
questions.explanation: Third order neurons in sensory pathways start in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus and project via internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2).
questions.keyConcept: Third order somatosensory neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which ventricle develops from the rhombencephalon?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle develops from the rhombencephalon (hindbrain), specifically from the cavity of the metencephalon. The lateral ventricles develop from the telencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Fourth ventricle derives from the hindbrain (rhombencephalon) cavity.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following cranial nerves is attached to the posterior aspect of the brain stem:
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the posterior aspect of the brainstem, specifically from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Trochlear nerve origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The representational (non‑dominant) hemisphere in most people is described by which feature?
options: It is responsible for language comprehension.
It always lies in the left hemisphere.
It is concerned with analytical tasks.
questions.explanation: The representational (non-dominant) hemisphere in most people lies in the right hemisphere and is specialized for spatial and holistic processing.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The choroid plexus is present in all ventricles except:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct (connecting third and fourth ventricles) is a narrow channel lined with ependyma but lacks choroid plexus, making it distinct from all three ventricles which have choroid plexus for CSF production.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct lacks choroid plexus (only ventricles have it).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lower motor neuron lesion is characterized by:
questions.explanation: LMN lesion causes lost/absent tendon jerks due to direct muscle denervation, muscle atrophy, and loss of all muscle tone and reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: LMN lesion causes lost tendon jerks

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Cerebral medulla contain all the following except:
questions.explanation: The cerebral medulla contains afferent/efferent fibers, dentate nuclei, and Purkinje fiber axons; Purkinje cells themselves are in the cerebellar cortex, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral medulla contents

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cisterna magna of subarachnoid space is a name given to the:
questions.explanation: The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern located between the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.
questions.keyConcept: Cisterna magna location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A chain of successive tracts in CNS having the same function is called:
questions.explanation: A pathway is a chain of successive tracts in the CNS serving the same function. A fasciculus is a smaller bundle within a tract. A lemniscus is a specific ascending brainstem pathway. A commissure connects two sides of the CNS, and a decussation is a midline crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Pathway = chain of successive tracts with identical function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS having the same beginning, termination and function is called:
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS sharing the same origin, termination, and function. A pathway is a chain of tracts. A lemniscus is an ascending brainstem bundle. A commissure connects hemispheres, and a decussation is a crossing.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle with common origin, termination, and function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The lowermost soft part of the auricle of ear is called:
questions.explanation: The lobule is the soft, fleshy lower part of the auricle (earlobe). The tragus is the small pointed projection anterior to the ear canal. The concha is the bowl-shaped depression.
questions.keyConcept: Lobule = soft lower part of the auricle (earlobe)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sensation from the angle of mandible is carried by:
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the temple and anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve supplies skin over the angle of the mandible

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tumor from central part of upper lip would likely spread to which group of lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The central part of the upper lip drains primarily to the submandibular lymph nodes. The upper lip also drains to the submental nodes via lymphatic crossing. The buccal and parotid nodes drain more lateral facial regions.
questions.keyConcept: Central upper lip drains to submandibular lymph nodes

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Pain from ala of nose is carried by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) laterally and the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) at the tip.
questions.keyConcept: Ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and external nasal nerve (V1)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The non-hairy region of the temple is supplied by which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The zygomaticotemporal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplies the non-hairy skin of the temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp of the temple.
questions.keyConcept: Zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the non-hairy temple region

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following scalp nerves is derived from dorsal rami of spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It supplies the skin of the occipital region of the scalp. The auriculotemporal, great auricular, lesser occipital, and posterior auricular nerves are ventral ramus derivatives.
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve = dorsal ramus of C2

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The artery that lies above parotid duct is a direct branch of:
questions.explanation: The transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery (external carotid), runs above the parotid duct. The facial artery enters the face at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter.
questions.keyConcept: Transverse facial artery lies above the parotid duct

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Infection of lateral part of the upper eye lid leads to enlargement of which group of lymph nodes:
questions.explanation: The lateral part of the upper eyelid drains to the parotid (pre-auricular) lymph nodes. The medial part drains to the submandibular nodes.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid lymph nodes

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is sensory to the scalp behind the auricle?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and the scalp behind the auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies scalp behind the auricle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Retromandibular vein:
options: Is formed by union of maxillary & superficial temporal veins.
Is deep to facial nerve inside parotid gland.
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the maxillary and superficial temporal veins. It begins inside the parotid gland, is deep to the facial nerve, and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein = maxillary + superficial temporal; lies deep to facial nerve in parotid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi:
options: Is attached to medial palpebral ligament.
Is attached to lateral palpebral raphe.
Is a part of orbicularis oris.
questions.explanation: The lacrimal part of the orbicularis oculi is attached to the lacrimal sac and the posterior lacrimal crest. It helps drain tears by compression of the lacrimal sac.
questions.keyConcept: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches to lacrimal sac and aids tear drainage

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Mandibular nerve is sensory to:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) carries sensation from the lower lip (via the mental nerve), chin, temporal region, and anterior ear. It does not supply the upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or tip of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory supply includes the lower lip and chin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Pulse felt at antero-inferior angle of masseter is from which artery?
questions.explanation: The facial artery can be palpated as it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery pulse is palpable at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Bleeding in which layer of scalp causes black eye?
questions.explanation: Bleeding into the loose areolar connective tissue layer of the scalp allows blood to spread freely and gravitate into the eyelids via the subaponeurotic space, causing a black eye.
questions.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue layer bleeding causes black eye via gravitational spread

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards scalp, all are true EXCEPT:
options: Its wounds gap if aponeurosis is cut.
Its veins communicate with intracranial venous sinuses.
It contains a muscle of facial expression.
questions.explanation: The scalp has numerous sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles. Its rich vascularity means wounds bleed profusely, and aponeurotic wounds gape due to muscle pull.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp has abundant sebaceous glands; wounds bleed profusely and gape if aponeurosis is cut

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The plane of movement of scalp is between:
questions.explanation: The scalp moves as a single unit because the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and epicranial aponeurosis are firmly attached. The plane of movement is between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp movement occurs between epicranial aponeurosis and pericranium

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The large blood vessels of scalp run in:
questions.explanation: The large blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is richly vascularized and innervated.
questions.keyConcept: Blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The main sensory nerve of the upper lip is:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division, V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip, lower eyelid, and cheek.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The pulse felt in front of tragus of ear against zygomatic arch is the pulse of:
questions.explanation: The superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, can be palpated in front of the tragus of the ear against the zygomatic arch.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial temporal artery pulse is palpable anterior to the tragus against the zygomatic arch

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The muscle that causes firm closure of eyelids is:
questions.explanation: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi is responsible for firm (forced) closure of the eyelids. The palpebral part closes the eye gently.
questions.keyConcept: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi = forced eye closure; palpebral part = gentle closure

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards buccinator muscle, all the following is true EXCEPT:
options: It is the muscle of the cheecks.
It arises from maxilla and mandible.
It is inserted in upper and lower lips.
It prevents accumulation of food in oral vestibule.
It is innervated by mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve.
questions.explanation: The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) via its buccal branches. It is NOT innervated by the mandibular nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the mandibular nerve

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the subcutaneous connective tissue layer of scalp, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It contains arteries & nerves of scalp.
It connects skin of scalp with aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis.
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous connective tissue layer of the scalp is dense and fibrous. Infections here are localized because the tissue is dense. Wounds bleed profusely because fibrous septa prevent vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous connective tissue of scalp is dense; infection is localized and wounds bleed profusely

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Injury of the right cortico-bulbar tract would affect muscles of:
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract controls lower facial muscles contralaterally. Lesion of the right corticobulbar tract causes paralysis of the left lower face (contralateral to the lesion).
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has contralateral control of lower face

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lesion of which cerebral area in left hemisphere causes motor aphasia?
questions.explanation: Motor aphasia (Broca's aphasia) results from lesion of Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which is responsible for speech production. In the dominant hemisphere, this is typically the left side.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area in inferior frontal gyrus causes motor aphasia

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Motor aphasia is due to lesion of the following area:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and is responsible for motor (expressive) speech. Lesions cause non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area - motor/expressive speech area

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Changes in personality and judgment occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex (anterior to the precentral gyrus) is responsible for personality, judgment, executive function, and social behavior. Lesions cause changes in personality and impaired judgment.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal area controls personality and judgment

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Injury to the left paracentral lobule leads to paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule is the continuation of the primary motor and sensory areas onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. The left paracentral lobule controls the right lower limb (leg and foot) via the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Left paracentral lobule controls right leg

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Changes in judgment & intelligence occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, is responsible for higher cognitive functions including judgment, reasoning, planning, and personality expression. These functions are lost in frontal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe controls judgment and intelligence

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The facial recognition areas are found in the undersurface of:
questions.explanation: The facial recognition areas (fusiform face area) are located on the undersurface of both temporal and occipital lobes. These areas specifically recognize familiar faces.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal and occipital undersurface

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with inability to understand words and speaks non understandable words. Lesion is most likely in Brodmann areas number:
questions.explanation: Brodmann areas 39 and 40 (angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus) in the dominant parietal-temporal region are responsible for language comprehension. Lesions cause Wernicke's receptive aphasia where speech is fluent but meaningless.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 39-40 lesion causes receptive aphasia

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The facial colliculus is formed by:
options: Abducent nucleus and facial nerve fibers.
Facial motor nucleus and abducent nerve fibers.
questions.explanation: The facial colliculus is formed by the abducent nucleus and the fibers of the facial nerve (motor root) that curve around it internally. These fibers form the facial nerve genu in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Facial colliculus formed by CN VI nucleus and CN VII fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following structures wind around cerebral peduncles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is an outpouching of the brain and does not wind around the cerebral peduncles; it runs in the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body. The trochlear nerve wraps around the cerebral peduncle.
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve does not wind around cerebral peduncle

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following form boundaries of interpeduncular fossa EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is not a boundary of the interpeduncular fossa. The boundaries are: cerebral peduncles (posterolateral), upper border of pons (inferior), optic chiasma (superior), and optic tract (posterolateral).
questions.keyConcept: Optic nerve not boundary of interpeduncular fossa

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: General visceral efferent column includes the following nuclei Except:
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus supplies muscles of the larynx. However, all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of X).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus supplies laryngeal muscles via X

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The special visceral efferent column of nuclei:
options: Supplies muscles derived from pharyngeal arches.
questions.explanation: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus belongs to the GVE (general visceral efferent) column, NOT the SVE column. The SVE column includes only the nucleus ambiguus (muscles of pharyngeal arch origin).
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus ambiguus involved in swallowing and speech

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nerve that emerges between the two heads of lateral pterygoid is:
questions.explanation: The buccal nerve is a sensory branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It emerges between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid muscle and supplies the skin of the cheek, buccal mucosa, and skin over the buccinator muscle. The inferior alveolar nerve descends deep to both heads, the masseteric nerve passes above the upper head, the lingual nerve descends between the medial pterygoid and mandible, and the auriculotemporal nerve emerges behind the temporomandibular joint.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve emerges between the two heads of lateral pterygoid muscle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The structure attached to the pterygoid hamulus is the:
questions.explanation: The pterygomandibular raphe is a tendinous band attached superiorly to the pterygoid hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate and inferiorly to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It represents the junction between the superior pharyngeal constrictor posteriorly and the buccinator anteriorly, serving as an important anatomical landmark during inferior alveolar nerve block anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygomandibular raphe is attached to the pterygoid hamulus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The pretracheal fascia is attached inferiority to:
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus. It is attached superiorly to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and inferiorly it extends into the superior mediastinum where it fuses with the fibrous pericardium and aortic arch adventitia. This allows infections inferior to the fascia to potentially spread into the mediastinum.
questions.keyConcept: Pretracheal fascia attaches inferiorly to pericardium/aortic adventitia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cervical fascia that forms the sheath of the parotid gland is the:
questions.explanation: The parotid gland is enclosed within a fibrous capsule formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia (the parotid sheath). This fascia is tough and limits the swelling of the inflamed parotid gland, causing severe pain during mumps. The superficial layer is dense, while the deep layer is thinner and attaches to the styloid process.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid sheath is formed by investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
