questions.explanation: Blood in the loose areolar tissue layer (subaponeurotic space) of the scalp can track around the orbit producing 'black eye' (periorbital ecchymosis).
questions.keyConcept: Black eye: hemorrhage in loose connective tissue layer of scalp.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which facial muscle receives only contralateral cortical innervation?
options: Orbicularis oculi of the upper face
Orbicularis oris of the lower face
questions.explanation: The mentalis muscle (chin) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Other lower facial muscles receive partial bilateral innervation, which is why upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral only innervation of lower face muscles distinguishes UMN from LMN facial palsy.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following direct tract except:
options: ventral reticulo-spinal tract and sulco-marginal tract
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal and rubrospinal tracts are indirect (multineuronal) tracts, while olivespinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, and sulcomarginal are direct.
questions.keyConcept: Direct vs indirect tracts

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has weakness of the right lower face, but can wrinkle his forehead symmetrically. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Preserved forehead wrinkling indicates intact upper motor neuron (UMN) innervation to the facial nucleus's upper face region; weakness of only the lower face indicates a UMN lesion affecting the contralateral corticobulbar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Lower face weakness with spared forehead: contralateral corticobulbar (UMN) lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lesion of facial nerve at stylomastoid foramen leads to:
options: Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of tongue.
Motor loss on the contralateral half of the face.
Motor loss on the ipsilateral half of face.
Loss of taste sensation from ipsilateral half of soft palate.
questions.explanation: A lesion at stylomastoid foramen causes lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting all muscles on that side, including the forehead (loss of frontalis and orbicularis oculi).
questions.keyConcept: Stylomastoid lesion: LMN facial paralysis (entire ipsilateral face).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which receptors are most likely responsible for the sudden muscle relaxation when a weight‑lifter releases a heavy load after a sustained hold?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs (type Ib) detect muscle tension and trigger inverse stretch reflex causing sudden muscle relaxation when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon reflex

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which descending motor pathway serves as an alternate route to the corticospinal tract?
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus, decussates immediately, and descends in the lateral funiculus. It serves as an accessory pathway for corticospinal function, particularly for flexor muscle control.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract is a crossed extrapyramidal pathway for motor control of distal limbs.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Pain from upper lip is carried by:
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve, a terminal branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), exits through the infraorbital foramen to supply skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the upper lip

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 45-years-old woman is suffering from numbness over the tip of her nose. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be damaged?
options: Anterior division of the mandibular nerve
Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
questions.explanation: The tip of the nose is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (ophthalmic division, V1). Therefore, numbness suggests damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Tip of the nose sensation = ophthalmic division (V1) via external nasal branch

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The branch of the mandibular nerve that supplies the scalp is the:
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, supplies the scalp in the temporal region and the skin over the anterior auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp via the temporal region

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The second order neuron in the pathway of pain from the face is:
questions.explanation: Pain from the face travels via the trigeminal nerve. The first order neuron cell bodies are in the trigeminal ganglion, second order neurons are in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of CN V carries face pain 2nd neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The corticonuclear tract has unilateral connections with:
questions.explanation: The corticonuclear tract has bilateral connections with most cranial nerve nuclei, except the lower facial nucleus (which is only contralateral) and the trochlear/trigeminal motor nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: Lower 7 facial nucleus has unilateral corticonuclear input

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the motor Decussation, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: It occurs in caudal part of medulla.
It is formed by internal arcuate fibers.
It shows the crossing of 20% of the fibers.
All of the above is true.
None of the above is true.
questions.explanation: Motor decussation (pyramidal decussation) occurs in the caudal part of the medulla, where about 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Motor decussation in caudal medulla

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards corticobulbar tract, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: It ends on contralateral cranial nerve nuclei only.
The part of facial nucleus that controls right half of orbicularis oris muscle receives left corticonuclear tract.
The left genioglossus muscle is controlled by right corticonuclear tract.
It forms a part of upper motor neuron.
questions.explanation: The corticobulbar tract ends on bilateral cranial nerve nuclei, not only contralateral. Some nuclei (like the lower facial) have predominantly contralateral input, but all have some bilateral contribution.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar has bilateral cranial nerve connections

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following olivary nuclear complex is not contained in medulla?
questions.explanation: The medial accessory olive is part of the olivary nuclear complex within the medulla. The superior olivary nucleus is in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus not in medulla

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei represents the visceral afferent column?
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius is the visceral afferent column. It receives taste (SVA) from anterior 2/3 tongue via chorda tympani (CN VII) and posterior 1/3 tongue via CN IX, and general visceral afferent (GVA) from thoracic and abdominal viscera via CN X.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor muscles supplied by CN V, not nucleus ambiguus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Special visceral afferent nuclei include:
questions.explanation: Special visceral afferent nuclei include the nucleus solitarius, which receives taste sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue (via chorda tympani, CN VII) and posterior 1/3 (via CN IX).
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) column includes:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the only pontine cranial nerve attached at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle, supplying the second pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) muscles.
questions.keyConcept: CN V attached at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards trigeminal ganglion, choose the INCORRECT statement:
options: Anterolaterally, it gives attachment to divisions of trigeminal nerve.
It lies at apex of petreous temporal bone.
Central processes of its cells form sensory root of trigeminal nerve.
questions.explanation: The trigeminal ganglion is INCORRECTLY described as lying at the apex of petrous temporal bone. It actually lies in Meckel's cave on the ANTERIOR surface of the petrous temporal bone, not at its apex.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion lies in Meckel's cave on the anterior surface of petrous temporal bone, not at the apex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from:
questions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion receives its parasympathetic preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus via the nervus intermedius, greater petrosal nerve, and facial nerve. These fibers continue in the chorda tympani nerve (branch of CN VII), which joins the lingual nerve and synapses in the submandibular ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then innervate the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. The lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX) supplies the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympathetic root to submandibular ganglion is derived from the chorda tympani nerve (CN VII).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following is a paired bone?
questions.explanation: The parietal bone is a PAIRED bone—there are two parietal bones, one on each side of the skull forming the lateral walls and roof of the cranial cavity. The frontal, occipital, and sphenoid bones are unpaired (single midline bones). The ethmoid is also unpaired, forming the nasal cavity and part of the orbit.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal bone is PAIRED (two parietal bones); forms lateral cranial wall. Frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid are unpaired.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 25 year old woman suffers from a traumatic scalp avulsion due to a revolving machinery at her workplace. All the following are considered boundaries for the scalp EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The scalp is bounded by: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (laterally), and supraorbital arch/ridge (anterior). The EXTERNAL OCCIPITAL PROTUBERANCE is a landmark on the skull but the scalp's posterior boundary is the superior nuchal line, not the protuberance itself. The zygomatic arch is the lateral boundary; zygomatic bone is part of the face, not a boundary of the scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Scalp boundaries: superior nuchal line (posterior), zygomatic arch (lateral), supraorbital arch (anterior). External occipital protuberance is a skull landmark, not scalp boundary.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following veins unite with a posterior branch of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein unites with the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.选项A正确. The answer is A. The external jugular drains the face and scalp.
questions.keyConcept: Retromandibular vein + posterior auricular vein = external jugular vein.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All are contents of infratemporal fossa Except:
questions.explanation: Infratemporal fossa contents: lateral pterygoid, medial pterygoid, maxillary artery, pterygoid venous plexus, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion.选项E正确. The answer is E. The pterygoid muscles and vessels are key contents.
questions.keyConcept: Infratemporal fossa: pterygoid muscles, maxillary artery, mandibular nerve, otic ganglion - NOT the orbit.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the relays nuclel of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus. The trapezoid body also passes through this area.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive (binaural hearing) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: What is the lateral lemniscus formed of?
options: Fibers from the nuclei of the trapezoid body
questions.explanation: The lateral lemniscus is formed from ALL THREE acoustic stria (dorsal, intermediate, and ventral) plus fibers from the superior olivary nucleus and trapezoid body nuclei. It carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral lemniscus: from all 3 acoustic stria + superior olive + trapezoid nuclei → inferior colliculus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure contains the first order neurons for facial pain and temperature?
questions.explanation: The trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian ganglion) contains first-order neurons for facial pain and temperature sensation. Central processes enter the pons and synapse in the spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion is the sensory ganglion for facial pain and temperature via cranial nerve V.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which area of the brain, when damaged, causes contralateral hemiplegia?
questions.explanation: The internal capsule contains descending corticospinal fibers that, when damaged, cause contralateral hemiplegia. Fibers are already crossed at the medullary pyramids, so internal capsule lesions affect the opposite side.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule damage causes contralateral motor deficits due to already-crossed corticospinal fibers.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has difficulty voluntarily moving both eyes to the right side. This deficit is most likely due to a lesion in which area?
questions.explanation: Horizontal gaze palsy indicates lesion in the abducens nucleus (CN VI) or PPRF (paramedian pontine reticular formation). The patient cannot voluntarily move eyes to the right, suggesting left PPRF/nucleus lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal gaze control localizes to the pons (PPRF/CN VI nucleus) for voluntary eye movements.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The medial geniculate body is connected to the brachium of which structure?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives auditory input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects to the primary auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: MG body connects to inferior colliculus via its brachium for auditory pathway.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Inferior salivatory nucleus supplies which of the following?
questions.explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the otic ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve (CN IX), which then innervates the parotid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior salivatory nucleus via CN IX controls parotid gland secretion through otic ganglion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which branch represents the only purely sensory nerve arising from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve?
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) is the only purely sensory branch of the anterior division of the trigeminal nerve, providing sensation to the orbit, forehead, and nose.
questions.keyConcept: V1 (ophthalmic nerve) is the sole purely sensory anterior division branch of CN V.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presents with painful vesicular eruptions localized to the chin and lower lip on one side of the face. Which nerve is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Painful vesicular eruptions in the trigeminal nerve distribution (V2/V3) suggest herpes zoster (shingles). The gasserian ganglion houses the cell bodies of trigeminal sensory neurons where the virus reactivates.
questions.keyConcept: Herpes zoster of trigeminal nerve reactivates in the gasserian ganglion, causing dermatomal vesicles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with pain localized to the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Which nerve primarily transmits sensory information from the TMJ?
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of V3) provides sensory innervation to the TMJ. It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland as well.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) innervates the TMJ and carries parasympathetic fibers to parotid.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which muscle lies lateral to the lateral pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle lies lateral to the lateral pterygoid muscle in the infratemporal fossa. It forms the muscular basis of the cheek and is innervated by the buccal branch of CN VII.
questions.keyConcept: Buccinator muscle is lateral to lateral pterygoid, forming the cheek wall in the infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure forms part of the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms part of the medial wall of the infratemporal fossa. It provides attachment for the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles and the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid plate contributes to the medial boundary of the infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the infratemporal fossa?
options: Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial boundary of the infratemporal fossa. The lateral boundary is the ramus of the mandible, and the roof is the greater wing of sphenoid.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid plate defines the medial limit of the infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which structure serves as the communication pathway between the infratemporal fossa and the pterygopalatine fossa?
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure serves as the communication between the infratemporal fossa and the pterygopalatine fossa, allowing passage of vessels and nerves including the maxillary artery and pterygopalatine nerve branches.
questions.keyConcept: Pterygomaxillary fissure connects infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae for neurovascular transmission.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nerve cell group have same function inside CNS:
questions.explanation: A nucleus is a collection of neuron cell bodies within the CNS that share a common origin and function, such as the red nucleus or substantia nigra.
questions.keyConcept: CNS nucleus definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nerve group cell outside CNS:
questions.explanation: A ganglion (plural: ganglia) is a collection of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS, such as dorsal root ganglia or autonomic ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Crossing of fibers from both sides in middle line:
questions.explanation: Decussation refers to the crossing of nerve fibers from both sides at the midline, such as the pyramidal decussation in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Decussation definition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of spino-tectal tract except:
options: arise from nerve cell in posterior horn (I,V)
ascend at all level of spinal on opposite side then tectum in mid brain
drive reflex, movement of eye, head
ascend in inferior olivary nucleus in medulla
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract arises from posterior horn cells (laminae I, V), ascends contralaterally to the superior colliculus for reflex eye/head movements, not the inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinotectal tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The first order neurons in proprioception pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains first order neurons for proprioception from the face, the only case of sensory neurons in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Facial proprioception neurons

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The second order neuron in simple touch pathway from face and head are in:
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for simple touch from the face are in the main (principal) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Facial touch second neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with defective pain, temperature, simple touch and proprioception sensations from one side of the face and scalp probably has lesion in:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus carries all sensory modalities from one side of the face; lesion causes contralateral facial sensory loss.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal lemniscus lesion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All of the following structures wind around the cerebral peduncle except:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve does not wind around the cerebral peduncle; optic tract, trochlear nerve, posterior cerebral artery, and basal vein do.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral peduncle relations

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The second order neuron for pain and temperature from the face is located in the:
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature sensation from the face is carried by the trigeminal nerve to the spinal nucleus of V (caudal part), which is the second-order neuron for this pathway before crossing to the contralateral side.
questions.keyConcept: Pain/temperature from face: second-order neuron in spinal nucleus of V.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The maxillary nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) exits the skull through the foramen rotundum, passing from the middle cranial fossa into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve exits via foramen rotundum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus is located in the medulla oblongata, receiving input from the spinal cord and cerebral cortex and sending climbing fiber projections to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior olivary nucleus: located in medulla oblongata.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The medial geniculate body is part of the auditory pathway and receives input from the:
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus, serving as the thalamic relay for the auditory pathway to the auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body receives input from inferior colliculus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The first-order neuron carrying pain and temperature from the face lies in the:
options: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
questions.explanation: Cell bodies are in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Pain and temperature first-order neuron: pseudounipolar cell body in trigeminal ganglion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: On the medial surface of the infratemporal fossa lies the:
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid plate forms the medial wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral pterygoid muscle lies on medial surface of infratemporal fossa.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All the following are true about the middle meningeal artery EXCEPT:
options: It is the largest meningeal artery.
It is a branch from 1st part of maxillary artery.
It enters the cranial cavity through foramen ovale.
It gives frontal and parietal terminal branches.
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through foramen spinosum (not ovale), making it vulnerable to fractures in the temporal region causing epidural hematoma.
questions.keyConcept: Middle meningeal artery: enters via foramen spinosum, not ovale.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The mandibular nerve reaches the infratemporal fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) passes from the middle cranial fossa to the infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.
questions.keyConcept: Mandibular nerve enters infratemporal fossa through foramen ovale.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Middle meningeal artery is encircled by roots of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve encircles the middle meningeal artery with its two roots, forming a neural loop around the vessel in the infratemporal fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Auriculotemporal nerve encircles middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Maxillary nerve reaches the pterygopalatine fossa through foramen:
questions.explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) passes from the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa before continuing as the infraorbital nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Maxillary nerve reaches pterygopalatine fossa through foramen rotundum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A pontine cranial nerve that is not attached to lower border of pons:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is attached to the lateral surface of the pons, at the junction of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. The abducent nerve attaches at the lower border, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal attaches at pons-middle cerebellar peduncle junction

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve has the following functional component:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the only nucleus in the CNS that contains pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies. It carries proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication and other structures, making it a General Somatic Afferent (GSA) nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Medial longitudinal bundle coordinates vestibular-eye reflexes

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The parasympathetic nucleus of the ninth cranial nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the inferior salivatory nucleus. It provides parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: SVE column supplies pharyngeal arch muscles

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following cranial nerve nuclei is not connected to the medial longitudinal bundle:
questions.explanation: This matching tests cranial nerve nuclei columns: SE - somatic muscles (III,IV,VI,XII); SVE - pharyngeal arch muscles (V,VII,IX,X,XI); GVE - parasympathetic (III,VII,IX,X).
questions.keyConcept: SVE column supplies pharyngeal arch derived muscles

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nerves supplying the scalp and face is not derived from the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The greater occipital nerve (C2) is NOT derived from the trigeminal nerve - it's a dorsal ramus of C2.选项A正确. The answer is A. It supplies the scalp posterior to the auricle.
questions.keyConcept: Greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) is the only scalp nerve not from trigeminal - supplies posterior scalp.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following cranial nerves contains sensory nerves fibers:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) contains sensory fibers for face, scalp, and oral cavity; the other listed nerves are purely motor.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal sensory function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which cranial nerve emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla oblongata between the pyramid and the olive?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the anterior aspect of the medulla between the pyramid and olive, carrying only motor fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoglossal nerve origin

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve belongs to which column of cranial nerve nuclei?
questions.explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is a special visceral efferent (SVE) nucleus, innervating muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch (muscles of mastication).
questions.keyConcept: Motor nucleus of V is special visceral efferent (SVE).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The facial nerve leaves the cranial cavity by passing through:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) exits the cranial cavity through the stylomastoid foramen located between the styloid and mastoid processes.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve exits via stylomastoid foramen.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem form:
questions.explanation: A lemniscus is a collection of sensory fibers that ascend through the brainstem. Examples include the medial lemniscus (fine touch/proprioception), spinal lemniscus (pain/temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation).
questions.keyConcept: Lemniscus is collection of ascending fibers in brainstem

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the medulla oblongata, the medial zone containing the pyramid is supplied by:
questions.explanation: The medial zone of the medulla (containing the pyramid) is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, which runs in the anterior median fissure. The lateral and posterior regions are supplied by vertebral artery branches and PICA.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal supplies medial medulla/pyramid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 30-year-old patient comes to the emergency room with a laceration on the scalp following a head injury. The wound appears to be bleeding profusely. Which layer of the scalp is primarily responsible for this bleeding?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of the scalp is highly vascular because it contains the arteries and veins of the scalp embedded in a firm fatty layer. This layer has rich anastomoses between the supraorbital, superficial temporal, and occipital arteries. The skin containsplexuses but the profuse bleeding in scalp lacerations is mainly from this highly vascular subcutaneous layer. The galea'subgaleal layer is avascular and the pericranium is thin.
questions.keyConcept: Subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) of scalp is highly vascular; main source of profuse bleeding in scalp injuries due to arterial anastomoses.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for retraction of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The masseter muscle retracts the mandible (pulls it posteriorly). The temporalis also retracts, while the medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid (lower head) protract the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Masseter is the primary mandibular retractor; temporalis assists with retrusion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding lamination of lateral corticospinal tract in brain stem, select the most medial fibers:
questions.explanation: In the brainstem, the lateral corticospinal tract fibers are organized somatotopically with cervical fibers most lateral and sacral fibers most medial. This is the reverse of their spinal cord arrangement.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers most medial in LCST at brainstem

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 65-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of inability to close her right eye. The patient noticed this problem a few days ago and it has been getting worse gradually. She also reports that her right eyelid droops and that she has difficulty smiling on the right side of her face. She has no other medical problems and is not taking any medications. Which of the following muscles is most likely affecting the chief complaint in this patient?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oculi is the muscle responsible for eye closure. It has three parts: palpebral (gentle closure), orbital (forced closure), and lacrimal (dilates lacrimal sac). Difficulty closing the eye (lagophthalmos), drooping eyelid, and inability to smile fully are classic signs of facial nerve palsy affecting the orbicularis oculi and other facial muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; weakness of eye closure + drooping eyelid + mouth deviation = facial nerve palsy.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Reflex cough accompanying ear wash is caused by irritation of ……… nerve.
questions.explanation: The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve) innervates the external acoustic meatus; its irritation during ear washing triggers the cough reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Ear wash cough reflex: auricular branch of vagus nerve.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking and swallowing. On examination, he has atrophy and deviation of the tongue to the right side. He also shows loss of vibration and proprioception on the left side of his body and loss of pain and temperature on the left side of his body. Most likely site of lesion:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and GI tract. Damage causes dysphagia (swallowing difficulty) and dysphonia (voice changes) due to loss of laryngeal innervation.
questions.keyConcept: CN X parasympathetic fibers control GI motility and cardiac rhythm; damage causes dysphagia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with sudden difficulty in comprehending spoken language. They can speak fluently, but their speech lacks meaningful content. Which area of the brain is most likely affected in this case?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) of the dominant hemisphere. It is responsible for language comprehension. Damage causes receptive (sensory) aphasia—fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. The patient speaks fluently but cannot understand others.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) = language comprehension; lesion causes receptive/sensory aphasia.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from:
questions.explanation: Ventral external arcuate fibers arise from the ARCUATE NUCLEUS (not the cuneate nucleus which projects to cerebellum via dorsal external arcuate fibers). The arcuate nucleus receives corticofugal fibers and projects to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral external arcuate: from arcuate nucleus → cerebellum (via ICP). Dorsal external arcuate: from accessory cuneate → cerebellum.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: A patient shows definite weakness of the right facial muscles while facial skin sensation is normal. On testing of the ocular movements, there is evidence of slight weakness of the right lateral rectus muscle. Radiology reveals the presence of tumour. Locate the possible site of the tumour.
options: Closed medulla at level of motor decussation.
questions.explanation: Inferior pons lesion affecting CN VI nucleus causes facial weakness (CN VII) and lateral rectus weakness (CN VI), with normal sensation pointing to a pontine tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior pons lesion

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The most of V nerve nuclei are best seen in:
questions.explanation: The main sensory and spinal nuclei of the trigeminal nerve are best seen in the upper pons at the level of the entry of the trigeminal nerve. The mesencephalic nucleus extends into the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve nuclei best seen in upper pons (entry zone)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connect between:
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract connects the red nucleus (midbrain) to the inferior olivary nucleus (medulla). It carries rubroreticular and reticuloolivary fibers. This pathway is important for motor learning and coordination.
questions.keyConcept: Central tegmental tract: red nucleus ↔ inferior olivary nucleus (olivocerebellar pathway).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: In the CNS Injury, which of the following cells are abundant:
questions.explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.
questions.keyConcept: CNS injury response: astrocyte proliferation (gliosis) + microglia activation (phagocytosis).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about microglia?
options: They are present in the retina and optic nerve
They are small spindle shaped cells with branching poles
The cell body and processes have minute spines on their surfaces
questions.explanation: Microglia are present in CNS including retina and optic nerve (CNS outgrowths). They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles and fine spines on their surfaces. They are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages, spindle-shaped with branched spiny processes, mesodermal origin.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Cerebral cortex is characterized by:
options: Layers of the same thickness all over the brain
questions.explanation: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar (functional minicolumns) organization. It has a folded surface (gyri and sulci), varying thickness, different neuron shapes in different layers, and shows plasticity.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex: 6 layers, columnar organization, folded surface, varying thickness, high plasticity.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: All of the following statements are correctly describing the pyramidal cells except:
options: The apex is directed to the cortical surface, a thick branching dendrite arises from the base of the cell and passes into the underlying white matter.
They are well developed in motor centers.
questions.explanation: In pyramidal cells, the APEX (where the thick branching dendrite arises) is directed INWARD toward the white matter, and the BASE is directed toward the cortical surface. The axon emerges from the base. Betz cells are indeed giant pyramidal cells in the motor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Pyramidal cell orientation: apex (dendrite) faces inward (white matter); base (axon) faces outward (surface).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The central gray in upper closed medulla contains:
questions.explanation: The central gray (around the central canal) in the upper closed medulla contains the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. At this level, it is continuous with the spinal nucleus in the medulla. The nucleus solitarius is more lateral.
questions.keyConcept: Central gray upper medulla: spinal nucleus of V. More laterally: nucleus solitarius. Ventrally: inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal, equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord, processing pain and temperature sensation from the face. It extends from the pons to the upper cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of trigeminal equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (pain/temperature)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve:
options: Formed of 2nd order neuron of proprioception from face.
Extend in the midbrain in the level of inferior colliculus only.
Contain 1st order neurons of pain from face.
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve contains pseudo-unipolar neurons (first-order neurons) for proprioception from face, muscles, and temporomandibular joint. It is the only sensory nucleus with cell bodies in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus contains pseudo-unipolar neurons for facial proprioception (1st order)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cranial nerves with nuclei in the medulla are IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal). The facial nerve (VII) has its nuclei in the pons, not the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve (VII) has nuclei in pons, NOT medulla - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the relays nuclei of auditory pathway is:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus is a relay nucleus in the auditory pathway, located in the pons. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei and projects to the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Superior olivary nucleus is a relay in auditory pathway (pons)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting between:
questions.explanation: The central tegmental tract contains fibers connecting the red nucleus to the inferior olivary nucleus. It is involved in the dentato-rubro-olivary circuit that modulates cerebellar function.
questions.keyConcept: Central tegmental tract connects red nucleus to inferior olivary nucleus

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei receive the GSA fibers of facial nerve:
questions.explanation: GSA (general somatic afferent) fibers of the facial nerve carry proprioception from facial muscles and sensation from a small area of the external ear. These fibers relay in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, which spans the pons and medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Facial nerve GSA: relays in spinal nucleus of trigeminal (same as other facial sensation).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Nuclei of the vagus nerve include the following except:
questions.explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus. The vagus has: nucleus ambiguus (branchial GSE), dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (GVE), and solitary nucleus (SVA, GVA).
questions.keyConcept: Vagus nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (motor), dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic), solitary nucleus (sensory).

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Cranial nerves in medulla oblongata are the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges from the PONS (at pontomedullary junction), not the medulla. The medullary cranial nerves are: IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal).
questions.keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI, XII. CN VII (facial) is pontine.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Gracile & Cuneate N. are present in:
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate nuclei are present on the DORSAL aspect of the closed medulla, forming the tubercles seen on the posterior surface. These nuclei receive proprioception and fine touch from the lower and upper body respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate nuclei: dorsal closed medulla; receive proprioception and fine touch.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Lowermost level of medulla shows:
questions.explanation: The lowermost medulla (near spinomedullary junction) shows the DECUSSATION OF CORTICOSPINAL FIBERS (motor decussation). The pyramids are not yet formed. The inferior olivary nucleus appears at higher (open medulla) levels. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Corticospinal decussation: lowermost medulla (motor decussation). Sensory decussation is higher. Olivary nucleus is higher still.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Basis pontis contain the following except:
questions.explanation: Basis pontis contains corticospinal fibers, corticonuclear fibers, transverse pontine fibers, and pontine nuclei. Pontine reticulospinal fibers are in the TEGMENTUM, not basis pontis.
questions.keyConcept: Basis pontis: corticospinal, corticonuclear, transverse pontine fibers. Tegmentum: reticulospinal, sensory nuclei.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Auditory pathways contain the following except:
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus carries somatosensory information (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), not auditory information. Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → auditory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGB → auditory cortex.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Superior colliculus, all true except:
options: Give tectospinal tract & dorsal tegmental decussation.
Present in tectum of the upper midbrain.
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus is NOT directly connected to the occipital cortex - that connection is via the visual cortex and lateral geniculate body. The superior colliculus is connected to the retina (via retinal ganglion cells), and gives rise to the tectospinal tract and dorsal tegmental decussation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus: connected to retina, not occipital cortex; gives tectospinal and dorsal tegmental decussation.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Fibers derived from which nucleus run transversally to form the trapezoid body?
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL cochlear nucleus gives rise to fibers that cross transversely to form the trapezoid body in the pons. These are part of the auditory pathway to the superior olivary nucleus. The dorsal cochlear nucleus projects via the intermediate acoustic stria.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral cochlear nucleus → trapezoid body → superior olivary nucleus (auditory pathway).
